# Why Is the Sky Blue?

## For a 3-Year-Old

The sky is blue because of the sunlight! The sun sends white light up to the sky, and the air is full of tiny, tiny particles — like little bouncing balls. When the sunlight hits them, the light bounces around, and the blue bounces the most. That's why you see a lot of blue when you look up. It's like shaking a jar full of blue sprinkles — the blue ones fly around and cover everything!

## For a High Schooler

The sky is blue because of a phenomenon called **Rayleigh scattering**. Sunlight is white, but it's actually made up of all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it hits tiny gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). These molecules scatter the light in every direction.

Here's the important part: how much light gets scattered depends on its wavelength. Shorter wavelengths (blue, violet) get scattered much more than longer wavelengths (red, orange). The amount of scattering goes as 1/λ⁴, meaning blue light (wavelength around 450 nm) gets scattered roughly 10 times more strongly than red light (around 650 nm).

That's why blue light bounces around the atmosphere and reaches your eyes from every direction — so you see blue all over the sky. Red light mostly travels straight through, which is also why sunsets look red (when the sun is low, sunlight passes through more air and the blue gets scattered away, leaving the red).

A quick note: violet has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so it gets scattered even more. But the sky looks blue instead of violet because the sun emits less violet light and our eyes are much more sensitive to blue than violet.

## For a Physics PhD

The color of the sky is a consequence of **Rayleigh scattering** off atmospheric molecules in the geometric optics regime...

# Why Is the Sky Blue?

## For a 3-Year-Old

The sky is blue because of the sunshine! The Sun sends down white light, and up in the sky there are teeny-tiny little bits of air, like the tiniest grains of sand you can't even see. When the sunlight bumps into them, the light bounces around and around — and the blue light bounces the MOST. So when you look up, all that bouncing blue light comes to your eyes and makes the sky look blue. It's like shaking a jar full of blue sprinkles — the blue ones fly everywhere and cover everything!

## For a High Schooler

The sky is blue because of a phenomenon called **Rayleigh scattering**. Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. When that light enters the atmosphere, it hits the tiny gas molecules that make up the air (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). Those molecules knock the light around and send it off in every direction.

The key detail: how much a given color gets scattered depends on its wavelength. **Shorter wavelengths scatter much more than longer ones.** The strength of the scattering goes as **1/λ⁴** — so it's a very steep effect. Blue light (wavelength ~450 nm) gets scattered roughly 10× more strongly than red light (~650 nm). That's why blue bounces all over the sky and reaches your eyes from every direction, making the whole dome look blue. Red light mostly just passes straight through.

This same effect explains why sunsets are red: when the Sun is low on the horizon, its light travels through a much thicker slice of atmosphere, so most of the blue gets scattered out of the direct beam before it reaches you, leaving the reds and oranges.

One common follow-up question: violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so it scatters even more — so why isn't the sky violet? Two reasons: the Sun doesn't emit as much violet as blue, and our eyes are far more sensitive to blue than to violet.

## For a Physics PhD

The blue color of a clear atmosphere is a consequence of **Rayleigh scattering** — elastic scattering by particles whose size is much smaller than the incident wavelength. In a molecular atmosphere (N₂, O₂ with diameters ~0.3 nm ≪ λ ~ 400–700 nm), each molecule is polarized by the incident field (induced dipole **p** = α**E**) and re-radiates; the angular and wavelength dependence of that dipole radiation give the Rayleigh result.

The scattering cross section per molecule is

    σ(λ) = (8π³/3) · [(n² − 1)² / (N² λ⁴)] · f(K),   f(K) = 6(1 − K) / (6 + 7K)

where n is the refractive index, N the molecular number density, and K the depolarization ratio accounting for polarizability anisotropy (for air, K ≈ 0.03, so f(K) ≈ 0.93). The defining feature is the **σ ∝ 1/λ⁴** scaling.

For air at 550 nm this gives σ ≈ 4×10⁻³¹ m², i.e. a volume scattering coefficient α = σN ≈ 1×10⁻⁵ m⁻¹. Over a vertical column (column density ∫N dz ≈ 2.15×10²⁹ m⁻²) the **optical depth is τ ≈ 0.09 at 550 nm**, rising to roughly 0.15–0.2 at 450 nm. A single-scattering optical depth of order 0.1 is already sufficient for the diffuse sky to be strongly blue — you do not need a deep or multiple-scattering regime.

**Why blue and not violet:** the Rayleigh law alone would peak in the violet/UV. The perceived blue comes from the product of three factors: (1) the solar spectrum (~5800 K blackbody, falling off toward the violet/UV), (2) the ocular sensitivity function V(λ) (low in the violet), and (3) absorption of short-wavelength light by the ocular lens. Together these suppress the violet response, so the integrated sky spectrum peaks perceptually in the blue.

**Why sunsets are red:** a low Sun sends light through a slant path with airmass up to ~38× the vertical (1/sin θ). The transmitted beam is attenuated by e^(−τ(λ)/sin θ), which preferentially removes the short wavelengths from the direct Sun and transmits reds. The scattered blue is redirected away from the direct line of sight.

**Caveats and extensions:** (a) Near the horizon the sky whitens because of **multiple scattering** over long paths and the growing contribution of **Mie scattering** from aerosols (size parameter a ~ 1), whose cross section is far less wavelength dependent (weakly ~1/λ or flatter) and scatters more isotropically. (b) The Rayleigh phase function for unpolarized incident light is ∝ (1 + cos²θ), giving **100% linear polarization at 90°** — the basis of polarization filters and the classic "90° from the Sun" observation. (c) The color is atmosphere-dependent: Mars's CO₂ + dust-scattering atmosphere is pinkish-red, and Titan's thick hydrocarbon haze (with methane blue-light absorption) is orange.

# 为什么天空是蓝色的？ (Why is the sky blue?)

## 给3岁的小朋友 (For a 3-year-old child)

天空是蓝色的，因为阳光！太阳把白色的光洒下来，天上飘着无数 tiny tiny 空气微粒，比你肉眼能看到的最细小的沙粒还要小。阳光碰到它们后，光就会到处弹来弹去——而蓝光弹得最多。所以当你抬头看时，这些弹跳的蓝光就飞进你的眼睛，让天空看起来是蓝色的。就像摇晃一罐装满蓝色糖屑的罐子——蓝色的糖屑飞得到处都是，把一切都覆盖了！

## 给高中生 (For a high schooler)

天空是蓝色的，原因在于一种叫做**瑞利散射**（Rayleigh scattering）的现象。阳光看起来是白色的，但其实它是彩虹所有颜色混合在一起的结果。当光线进入大气层时，会撞上组成空气的微小气体分子（主要是氮气和氧气）。这些分子会把光撞得四散，朝各个方向发射出去。

关键细节在于：某种颜色被散射的程度取决于它的波长。**波长越短，散射得越强烈。**散射强度按 **1/λ⁴** 变化——这是一个非常陡峭的效应。蓝光（波长约450纳米）被散射的强度大约比红光（约650纳米）强10倍。正因如此，蓝光在天空中四处弹跳，从各个方向进入你的眼睛，让整个天空穹顶看起来都是蓝色的。红光则大部分直接穿透过去。

同样的效应也解释了为什么日落是红色的：当太阳靠近地平线时，阳光要穿过厚得多的大气层，因此在到达你眼睛之前，大部分蓝光已被散射出直射光束，只剩下红色和橙色。

一个常见的后续问题：紫光的波长比蓝光还短，所以它散射得更多——那为什么天空不是紫色的呢？原因有二：太阳发出的紫光没有蓝光那么多，而且我们的眼睛对蓝光的敏感度远高于紫光。

## 给物理学博士 (For a physics PhD)

晴朗大气的蓝色是**瑞利散射**的结果——即由尺寸远小于入射波长的粒子产生的弹性散射。在分子大气中（N₂、O₂ 的直径约 0.3 nm ≪ λ ~ 400–700 nm），每个分子都会被入射场极化（诱导偶极子 **p** = α**E**）并重新辐射；这种偶极辐射的角度依赖性和波长依赖性给出了瑞利散射的结果。

每个分子的散射截面为

    σ(λ) = (8π³/3) · [(n² − 1)² / (N² λ⁴)] · f(K),   f(K) = 6(1 − K) / (6 + 7K)

# 为什么天空是蓝色的？

## 给3岁的小朋友

天空是蓝色的，因为阳光！太阳把白色的光洒下来，天上飘着无数 tiny tiny 空气微粒，比你肉眼能看到的最细小的沙粒还要小。阳光碰到它们后，光就会到处弹来弹去——而蓝光弹得最多。所以当你抬头看时，这些弹跳的蓝光就飞进你的眼睛，让天空看起来是蓝色的。就像摇晃一罐装满蓝色糖屑的罐子——蓝色的糖屑飞得到处都是，把一切都覆盖了！

## 给高中生

天空是蓝色的，原因在于一种叫做**瑞利散射**（Rayleigh scattering）的现象。阳光看起来是白色的，但其实它是彩虹所有颜色混合在一起的结果。当光线进入大气层时，会撞上组成空气的微小气体分子（主要是氮气和氧气）。这些分子会把光撞得四散，朝各个方向发射出去。

关键细节在于：某种颜色被散射的程度取决于它的波长。**波长越短，散射得越强烈。**散射强度按 **1/λ⁴** 变化——这是一个非常陡峭的效应。蓝光（波长约450纳米）被散射的强度大约比红光（约650纳米）强10倍。正因如此，蓝光在天空中四处弹跳，从各个方向进入你的眼睛，让整个天空穹顶看起来都是蓝色的。红光则大部分直接穿透过去。

Why Is the Sky Blue?

为什么天空是蓝色的？

English

For a 3-Year-Old

The sky is blue because of the sunshine! The Sun sends down white light, and up in the sky there are teeny-tiny little bits of air, like the tiniest grains of sand you can't even see. When the sunlight bumps into them, the light bounces around and around — and the blue light bounces the MOST. So when you look up, all that bouncing blue light comes to your eyes and makes the sky look blue. It's like shaking a jar full of blue sprinkles — the blue ones fly everywhere and cover everything!

For a High Schooler

The sky is blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. When that light enters the atmosphere, it hits the tiny gas molecules that make up the air (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). Those molecules knock the light around and send it off in every direction.

The key detail: how much a given color gets scattered depends on its wavelength. Shorter wavelengths scatter much more than longer ones. The strength of the scattering goes as 1/λ⁴ — so it's a very steep effect. Blue light (wavelength ~450 nm) gets scattered roughly 10× more strongly than red light (~650 nm). That's why blue bounces all over the sky and reaches your eyes from every direction, making the whole dome look blue. Red light mostly just passes straight through.

This same effect explains why sunsets are red: when the Sun is low on the horizon, its light travels through a much thicker slice of atmosphere, so most of the blue gets scattered out of the direct beam before it reaches you, leaving the reds and oranges.

One common follow-up question: violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so it scatters even more — so why isn't the sky violet? Two reasons: the Sun doesn't emit as much violet as blue, and our eyes are far more sensitive to blue than to violet.

For a Physics PhD

The blue color of a clear atmosphere is a consequence of Rayleigh scattering — elastic scattering by particles whose size is much smaller than the incident wavelength. In a molecular atmosphere (N₂, O₂ with diameters ~0.3 nm ≪ λ ~ 400–700 nm), each molecule is polarized by the incident field (induced dipole p = αE) and re-radiates; the angular and wavelength dependence of that dipole radiation give the Rayleigh result.

σ(λ) = (8π³/3) · [(n² − 1)² / (N² λ⁴)] · f(K),   f(K) = 6(1 − K) / (6 + 7K)

where n is the refractive index, N the molecular number density, and K the depolarization ratio accounting for polarizability anisotropy (for air, K ≈ 0.03, so f(K) ≈ 0.93). The defining feature is the σ ∝ 1/λ⁴ scaling.

For air at 550 nm this gives σ ≈ 4×10⁻³¹ m², i.e. a volume scattering coefficient α = σN ≈ 1×10⁻⁵ m⁻¹. Over a vertical column (column density ∫N dz ≈ 2.15×10²⁹ m⁻²) the optical depth is τ ≈ 0.09 at 550 nm, rising to roughly 0.15–0.2 at 450 nm. A single-scattering optical depth of order 0.1 is already sufficient for the diffuse sky to be strongly blue — you do not need a deep or multiple-scattering regime.

Why blue and not violet: the Rayleigh law alone would peak in the violet/UV. The perceived blue comes from the product of three factors: (1) the solar spectrum (~5800 K blackbody, falling off toward the violet/UV), (2) the ocular sensitivity function V(λ) (low in the violet), and (3) absorption of short-wavelength light by the ocular lens. Together these suppress the violet response, so the integrated sky spectrum peaks perceptually in the blue.

Why sunsets are red: a low Sun sends light through a slant path with airmass up to ~38× the vertical (1/sin θ). The transmitted beam is attenuated by e^(−τ(λ)/sin θ), which preferentially removes the short wavelengths from the direct Sun and transmits reds. The scattered blue is redirected away from the direct line of sight.

Caveats and extensions: (a) Near the horizon the sky whitens because of multiple scattering over long paths and the growing contribution of Mie scattering from aerosols (size parameter a ~ 1), whose cross section is far less wavelength dependent (weakly ~1/λ or flatter) and scatters more isotropically. (b) The Rayleigh phase function for unpolarized incident light is ∝ (1 + cos²θ), giving 100% linear polarization at 90° — the basis of polarization filters and the classic "90° from the Sun" observation. (c) The color is atmosphere-dependent: Mars's CO₂ + dust-scattering atmosphere is pinkish-red, and Titan's thick hydrocarbon haze (with methane blue-light absorption) is orange.

# Why Is the Sky Blue? · 为什么天空是蓝色的？

## For a 3-Year-Old / 给3岁的小朋友

### English

The sky is blue because of the sunshine! The Sun sends down white light, and up in the sky there are teeny-tiny little bits of air, like the tiniest grains of sand you can't even see. When the sunlight bumps into them, the light bounces around and around — and the blue light bounces the MOST. So when you look up, all that bouncing blue light comes to your eyes and makes the sky look blue. It's like shaking a jar full of blue sprinkles — the blue ones fly everywhere and cover everything!

### 中文

天空是蓝色的，因为阳光！太阳把白色的光洒下来，天上飘着无数超超小的空气微粒，比你肉眼能看到的最细小的沙粒还要小。阳光碰到它们后，光就会到处弹来弹去——而蓝光弹得最多。所以当你抬头看时，这些弹跳的蓝光就飞进你的眼睛，让天空看起来是蓝色的。就像摇晃一罐装满蓝色糖屑的罐子——蓝色的糖屑飞得到处都是，把一切都覆盖了！

## For a High Schooler / 给高中生

### English

The sky is blue because of a phenomenon called **Rayleigh scattering**. Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. When that light enters the atmosphere, it hits the tiny gas molecules that make up the air (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). Those molecules knock the light around and send it off in every direction.

The key detail: how much a given color gets scattered depends on its wavelength. **Shorter wavelengths scatter much more than longer ones.** The strength of the scattering goes as **1/λ⁴** — so it's a very steep effect. Blue light (wavelength ~450 nm) gets scattered roughly 10× more strongly than red light (~650 nm). That's why blue bounces all over the sky and reaches your eyes from every direction, making the whole dome look blue. Red light mostly just passes straight through.

This same effect explains why sunsets are red: when the Sun is low on the horizon, its light travels through a much thicker slice of atmosphere, so most of the blue gets scattered out of the direct beam before it reaches you, leaving the reds and oranges.

One common follow-up question: violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so it scatters even more — so why isn't the sky violet? Two reasons: the Sun doesn't emit as much violet as blue, and our eyes are far more sensitive to blue than to violet.

### 中文

天空是蓝色的，原因在于一种叫做**瑞利散射**（Rayleigh scattering）的现象。阳光看起来是白色的，但其实它是彩虹所有颜色混合在一起的结果。当光线进入大气层时，会撞上组成空气的微小气体分子（主要是氮气和氧气）。这些分子会把光撞得四散，朝各个方向发射出去。

关键细节在于：某种颜色被散射的程度取决于它的波长。**波长越短，散射得越强烈。**散射强度按 **1/λ⁴** 变化——这是一个非常陡峭的效应。蓝光（波长约450纳米）被散射的强度大约比红光（约650纳米）强10倍。正因如此，蓝光在天空中四处弹跳，从各个方向进入你的眼睛，让整个天空穹顶看起来都是蓝色的。红光则大部分直接穿透过去。

同样的效应也解释了为什么日落是红色的：当太阳靠近地平线时，阳光要穿过厚得多的大气层，因此在到达你眼睛之前，大部分蓝光已被散射出直射光束，只剩下红色和橙色。

一个常见的后续问题：紫光的波长比蓝光还短，所以它散射得更多——那为什么天空不是紫色的呢？原因有二：太阳发出的紫光没有蓝光那么多，而且我们的眼睛对蓝光的敏感度远高于紫光。

## For a Physics PhD / 给物理学博士

### English

The blue color of a clear atmosphere is a consequence of **Rayleigh scattering** — elastic scattering by particles whose size is much smaller than the incident wavelength. In a molecular atmosphere (N₂, O₂ with diameters ~0.3 nm ≪ λ ~ 400–700 nm), each molecule is polarized by the incident field (induced dipole **p** = α**E**) and re-radiates; the angular and wavelength dependence of that dipole radiation give the Rayleigh result.

The scattering cross section per molecule is

    σ(λ) = (8π³/3) · [(n² − 1)² / (N² λ⁴)] · f(K),   f(K) = 6(1 − K) / (6 + 7K)

where n is the refractive index, N the molecular number density, and K the depolarization ratio accounting for polarizability anisotropy (for air, K ≈ 0.03, so f(K) ≈ 0.93). The defining feature is the **σ ∝ 1/λ⁴** scaling.

For air at 550 nm this gives σ ≈ 4×10⁻³¹ m², i.e. a volume scattering coefficient α = σN ≈ 1×10⁻⁵ m⁻¹. Over a vertical column (column density ∫N dz ≈ 2.15×10²⁹ m⁻²) the **optical depth is τ ≈ 0.09 at 550 nm**, rising to roughly 0.15–0.2 at 450 nm. A single-scattering optical depth of order 0.1 is already sufficient for the diffuse sky to be strongly blue — you do not need a deep or multiple-scattering regime.

**Why blue and not violet:** the Rayleigh law alone would peak in the violet/UV. The perceived blue comes from the product of three factors: (1) the solar spectrum (~5800 K blackbody, falling off toward the violet/UV), (2) the ocular sensitivity function V(λ) (low in the violet), and (3) absorption of short-wavelength light by the ocular lens. Together these suppress the violet response, so the integrated sky spectrum peaks perceptually in the blue.

**Why sunsets are red:** a low Sun sends light through a slant path with airmass up to ~38× the vertical (1/sin θ). The transmitted beam is attenuated by e^(−τ(λ)/sin θ), which preferentially removes the short wavelengths from the direct Sun and transmits reds. The scattered blue is redirected away from the direct line of sight.

**Caveats and extensions:** (a) Near the horizon the sky whitens because of **multiple scattering** over long paths and the growing contribution of **Mie scattering** from aerosols (size parameter a ~ 1), whose cross section is far less wavelength dependent (weakly ~1/λ or flatter) and scatters more isotropically. (b) The Rayleigh phase function for unpolarized incident light is ∝ (1 + cos²θ), giving **100% linear polarization at 90°** — the basis of polarization filters and the classic "90° from the Sun" observation. (c) The color is atmosphere-dependent: Mars's CO₂ + dust-scattering atmosphere is pinkish-red, and Titan's thick hydrocarbon haze (with methane blue-light absorption) is orange.

### 中文

晴朗大气的蓝色是**瑞利散射**的结果——即由尺寸远小于入射波长的粒子产生的弹性散射。在分子大气中（N₂、O₂ 的直径约 0.3 nm ≪ λ ~ 400–700 nm），每个分子都会被入射场极化（诱导偶极子 **p** = α**E**）并重新辐射；这种偶极辐射的角度依赖性和波长依赖性给出了瑞利散射的结果。

每个分子的散射截面为

    σ(λ) = (8π³/3) · [(n² − 1)² / (N² λ⁴)] · f(K),   f(K) = 6(1 − K) / (6 + 7K)

其中 n 是折射率，N 是分子数密度，K 是去偏振比，用于描述极化率的各向异性（对于空气，K ≈ 0.03，因此 f(K) ≈ 0.93）。其决定性特征是 **σ ∝ 1/λ⁴** 的标度关系。

对于 550 nm 处的空气，可得 σ ≈ 4×10⁻³¹ m²，即体散射系数 α = σN ≈ 1×10⁻⁵ m⁻¹。沿垂直方向积分（柱密度 ∫N dz ≈ 2.15×10²⁹ m⁻²），**550 nm 处的光学厚度 τ ≈ 0.09**，在 450 nm 处上升到约 0.15–0.2。量级为 0.1 的单次散射光学厚度就足以让漫射天空呈现明显的蓝色——无需进入深散射或多重散射区域。

**为什么是蓝色而不是紫色：**单靠瑞利定律，峰值应落在紫光/紫外区。我们感知到的蓝色来自三个因子的乘积：(1) 太阳光谱（约5800 K 的黑体，向紫光/紫外方向衰减），(2) 眼睛的敏感度函数 V(λ)（在紫光区较低），(3) 眼晶状体对短波长光的吸收。这三者共同抑制了对紫光的响应，因此天空积分光谱在感知上峰值落在蓝色。

**为什么日落是红色：**低空太阳的光线沿斜路径穿过大气，气团质量（airmass）最多可达垂直方向的约38倍（1/sin θ）。透射光束按 e^(−τ(λ)/sin θ) 衰减，这优先去除了直射阳光中的短波长成分，透射以红色为主。被散射的蓝光被偏转离开直射视线方向。

**注意事项与扩展：**(a) 靠近地平线时天空变白，这是因为长路径上的**多重散射**，以及气溶胶（尺寸参数 a ~ 1）**米氏散射**贡献的增加；后者截面随波长的依赖要弱得多（弱 ~1/λ 或更平坦），且散射更接近各向同性。(b) 对非偏振入射光，瑞利相位函数 ∝ (1 + cos²θ)，在 **90° 处线偏振度达 100%**——这是偏振滤光片以及经典"距太阳90°"观测的基础。(c) 天空颜色取决于大气成分：火星的 CO₂ + 尘埃散射大气呈粉红色；土星卫星泰坦（土卫六）厚厚的碳氢化合物雾霭（甲烷吸收蓝光）呈橙色。

import csv
from collections import defaultdict

spend = defaultdict(float)
names = {}

with open("bookstore_orders.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        cust = row["customer_id"]
        # Skip orders that were never actually paid (declined/cancelled)

        names[cust] = f"{row['customer_first_name']} {row['customer_last_name']}"
        spend[cust] += float(row["order_grand_total"])
        if row["return_requested"] == "Yes":
            spend[cust] -= float(row["refund_amount"])

top10 = sorted(spend.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)[:10]

with open("top-cust.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["FullName", "TotalSpend"])
    for cust, total in top10:
        w.writerow([names[cust], f"{total:.2f}"])

import csv
from collections import defaultdict

genres = defaultdict(lambda: {"total": 0, "returned": 0, "refund": 0.0})

with open("bookstore_orders.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        g = genres[row["primary_item_genre"]]
        g["total"] += 1
        if row["return_requested"] == "Yes":

            g["refund"] += float(row["refund_amount"])

rows = []
for genre, g in genres.items():
    rate = round(g["returned"] / g["total"] * 100, 2)
    rows.append((genre, g["total"], g["returned"], rate, round(g["refund"], 2)))

rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r[3], r[4]), reverse=True)

with open("genre-returns.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["Genre", "TotalOrders", "ReturnedOrders", "ReturnRatePct", "TotalRefund"])
    for genre, total, returned, rate, refund in rows:
        w.writerow([genre, total, returned, f"{rate:.2f}", f"{refund:.2f}"])

import csv
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import datetime

times = defaultdict(list)
fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"

with open("bookstore_orders.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        if row["fulfillment_status"] != "Delivered":
            continue
        order_ts = datetime.strptime(row["order_timestamp"], fmt)
        actual_ts = datetime.strptime(row["actual_delivery_date"], fmt)
        hours = (actual_ts - order_ts).total_seconds() / 3600
        times[row["carrier_name"]].append(hours)

rows = []
for carrier, hrs in times.items():

rows.sort(key=lambda r: r[2])

with open("carrier-delivery-time.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["CarrierName", "DeliveredOrders", "AvgDeliveryHours"])
    for carrier, count, avg in rows:
        w.writerow([carrier, count, f"{avg:.2f}"])

import csv
from collections import defaultdict

stats = defaultdict(lambda: {"count": 0, "gross": 0.0, "refunds": 0.0})

with open("bookstore_orders.csv", newline="") as f:

input.content:
# Latent Camera — Summary

"Latent Camera" (`com.pixelary.latent`) is a single-activity Android camera app built on Jetpack Compose (`MainActivity` hosts a Compose `MainScreen` wrapping an OpenGL ES `GLSurfaceView`). Rather than using the platform's processed preview, it captures **raw sensor images** via Camera2 (`SensorCapture`) and feeds them through a custom GPU image-processing pipeline (`LivePreview`, which acts as both GL renderer and ISP thread): demosaicing (CFA), black/white-level calibration, AWB white-balance gains, a 3x3 color matrix, lens distortion correction, auto-levels, and optional spatial denoise / false-color / highlight-recovery / log-tone stages. The UI is layered as a Compose `Scaffold` over the recordable EGL viewport, with a Compose settings overlay (`CameraSelectionOverlay`) and helper components for camera discovery (`CameraProvider`), MP4 encoding (`CaptureVideo`), ADPF/thread-priority performance tuning (`PerformanceOptimizer`), and GPS (`LocationTracker`).

Functionally, it is a pro-grade manual camera: tap or volume-up to capture stills (GL readback is read back on a background executor, then JPEG-encoded via MediaStore with full EXIF — ISO, shutter, focal length, aperture, GPS), long-press or volume-down to record MP4 video (with AWB locked during recording, a swipe-to-lock gesture, dropped-frame reporting, and async gallery save). It exposes manual ISO and shutter (with auto-snap to 50/60 Hz flicker periods), AE compensation, exposure lock, OIS, 1–10x digital zoom, lens/camera switching across grouped physical lenses, a comparison/"raw preview" mode, live ISO/shutter readouts, and a debug overlay (processing time, battery draw, thermal status). An external broadcast intent (`com.pixelary.latent.TOGGLE_VIDEO`) additionally allows hardware/remote shutter triggering, and the lifecycle logic handles camera teardown on pause and full state reset when switching lenses.

import os, struct
def png_chunks(path):
